title: microhotspot-sweep-and-eviction-horizon-notes
body:
Purpose:
This note captures an experimental sweep aimed at understanding small, ephemeral "microhotspots" in the KV residency set and the tradeoffs of different eviction horizon policies (short aggressive horizon vs. conservative horizon). Goal is actionable rules-of-thumb for an adaptive eviction governor that minimizes tail latency from NVMe/PCIe stalls while preserving aggregate reuse efficiency.

Background and motivation:
- We keep seeing brief bursts where a tiny subset of keys/slots get touched heavily for 10–200ms and then never again in a request stream. These produce spike fetches to NVMe/host memory that amplify latency for other simultaneous requests when bandwidth saturates.
- Existing eviction policies tuned for steady-state reuse distance (LRU-ish) either overprotect these microhotspots (pinning them and hurting new-hot reuse) or evict them quickly and suffer immediate re-population I/O.
- Idea: measure microhotspot lifetime distribution and the per-hotset fetch cost under contention; define an "eviction horizon" window (time-based) and experiment with adaptive heuristics.

Synthetic trace generator (how we simulate):
- base trace: real production sampled traces (1% sample over 24h) to get realistic key popularity distribution and multi-seqlen mixtures.
- microhotspot overlay: inject synthetic streaks that touch 32–512 keys at 50–5k qps for durations 20ms–400ms.
- concurrency model: 32 to 256 concurrent requests per GPU worker to stress memory bandwidth and NVMe plane occupancy.
- I/O model: measured NVMe p99 sequential read = 1.2ms, random read p99 = 5.8ms (lab cluster); bandwidth cap per host = 4.8 GB/s.

Instrumentation collected (per-run):
- reuse_rate_snapshot: fraction of requests satisfied from GPU memory vs host/ssd per 10ms bin
- eviction_events: timestamps, evicted_slot_id, reason (TTL/horizon/pressure), residency_time_ms
- pageback_latency: latency distribution for pages pulled from NVMe (30th/50th/90th/99th)
- memory_bandwidth_util: sampled every 5ms from perf counters (GB/s)
- request_tail_ms: request completion p50/p95/p99

Sweep matrix: (parameters varied)
- eviction_horizon_ms: [10, 50, 100, 250, 500]
- aggressive_threshold: fraction of hotset touches that must be observed before a slot is pinned [0.1, 0.3, 0.6]
- cold_eviction_backoff: cool-down time after a slot is evicted before it can be considered for pinning [20ms, 100ms, 500ms]
- nvme_bandwidth_throttle: ON/OFF (simulates noisy neighbor)

Representative run summary (selected rows):
1) horizon=10ms, threshold=0.3, backoff=20ms, throttle=OFF
- observations: microhotspots mostly get evicted quickly, reuse from GPU drops 6.2% relative to baseline, but steady-state memory_bandwidth_util reduces 12% and request p99 improves by ~7% (less background read contention). However frequent re-population causes more small I/O spikes scattered across time.

2) horizon=250ms, threshold=0.3, backoff=100ms, throttle=OFF
- observations: microhotspots are retained longer; reuse improves +4.9% vs baseline, memory_bandwidth_util increases 9% and p99 request latency increased by 18% during hotspot bursts (NVMe queueing). When burst durations exceed horizon < 250ms the policy helps, but when hotspot lifetime << horizon we waste residency and evict useful long-tail entries.

3) horizon=100ms, threshold=0.6, backoff=100ms, throttle=ON
- observations: raising threshold prevents pinning of short spikes; NVMe contention amplified under throttle, but p99 was better than 250ms horizon run. Suggests combining horizon with a conservatism factor (threshold) is necessary under noisy I/O.

Key quantitative signals (aggregated across runs):
- Microhotspot lifetime CDF: 60% < 50ms, 80% < 150ms, 95% < 350ms. (Implication: short horizons capture most ephemeral events; long horizons waste residency.)
- Eviction penalty (additional request latency when evicted then re-accessed) correlated with concurrent memory_bandwidth_util: when util > 70% penalty p99 multiplies by 2.8x vs util < 40% where penalty is ~1.4x.
- Optimal single static horizon (for our synthetic mix) in isolation: ~80–120ms minimizes combined cost metric (weighted 0.7*tail-latency + 0.3*miss-rate). But sensitivity is high under NVMe contention.

Observed failure modes and surprises:
- Back-to-back microhotspot waves: when two distinct microhotspots alternate quickly, short horizons cause oscillating evictions and read-amplification. The pattern is akin to aliasing; a tiny hysteresis/backoff reduces oscillation.
- Pinning threshold miscalibration: low threshold pins keys too eagerly (wastes cache), high threshold delays capturing real microhotspot that lasts slightly longer than horizon.
- Bank-level memory hotspots (NVMe parallelism): Many runs saw that bandwidth saturation was due to NVMe controller queue depth, not absolute GB/s; spreading reads temporally helps more than pure batching.

Heuristic proposals (practical, low-cost):
1) Adaptive horizon = base_horizon (80ms) * (1 + bandwidth_util_fraction * 1.2). Explanation: increase horizon when NVMe is underutilized to favor reuse; shrink horizon aggressively under high utilization.

2) Two-tiered pin decision:
- fast_candidate: observed touch density > X in sliding 50ms window -> assign candidate score;
- promote_to_pin only if candidate score persists for Y ms or if current bandwidth_util < 0.6. Otherwise treat as ephemeral and allow short eviction.

3) Cool-down guard for oscillation: after evicting a slot that had >N hits lifetime < M ms, apply randomized backoff (20–100ms) before reconsidering pin to avoid immediate thrash.

Operational runbook notes (for SRE):
- Telemetry to publish: microhotspot lifetime histogram, pin promotion rate, eviction oscillation rate (evict->repopulate within 2x horizon), and NVMe queue depth.
- Alerting: trigger when eviction oscillation rate > 8% for >10 minutes or when memory_bandwidth_util > 85% and p99 increases > 2x baseline.

Next experiments (short list):
- Real-traffic A/B with adaptive horizon heuristic + pin threshold on a small fleet segment (10% traffic) to validate user-visible p99 improvements.
- Microbenchmark to measure NVMe controller queue depth behavior: hold constant GB/s but vary IOPS pattern (many small random reads vs few large sequential reads) to isolate controller-level saturation effects.
- Evaluate combining horizon with selective compression of rarely-used slots to free capacity without full eviction (cheap transient compression).

Open questions / TODOs:
- What is a good default weight for the combined metric (tail vs miss-rate) that matches product SLOs? Product might want more conservative tail protection.
- How to integrate with multi-tenant fairness? An adaptive horizon that leverages per-tenant bandwidth share may be needed.
- Need microsecond-resolution tracing to see intra-request impact for batching scenarios; current 5–10ms bins hide some interleaving effects.

Appendix: raw sample numbers from a 15-minute run (horizon=100ms, threshold=0.3):
- total requests: 3,162,000
- gpu_satisfied: 2,874,300 (90.9%)
- host_ssd_satisfied: 287,700 (9.1%)
- p50 latency: 11.4ms; p95: 34.7ms; p99: 128.9ms
- avg mem_bandwidth_util: 61% (peaks 89% during hotspot waves)
- eviction_oscillation_rate: 4.3%

Notes to reviewers / quick decisions requested:
- Please sanity-check the lifetime CDF and whether it matches what you see in your production traces (Robin - can you attach sample_trace_2024-10-30?).
- If SRE agrees, I can schedule a small canary with the adaptive horizon heuristic for next Tuesday's capacity window.

End of note.

(Maya)
